title: Africa’s green industrialization blind spot: coordination
body:
Africa does not lack green resources. It does not lack ambition.

What most African countries lack is coordination capacity.

Green industrialization is not a single-ministry project. It breaks down when:

- Energy plans are designed without industrial demand
- Mining policy stops at extraction and ignores processing and value addition
- Trade policy undercuts domestic green producers
- Regulators optimise for compliance, not competitiveness

When ministries act in silos, green industrialization becomes fragmented—technically sound on paper, economically fragile in practice.

Factories do not run on “efficient markets” alone. They simultaneously need long-term power contracts, predictable pricing, and reliable grids, among others.

- This emerges only where states can coordinate policy, institutions, and incentives over time.
- Green industrialization is, thus, as much an institutional challenge as it is a technological one.

African countries that will emerge as green industrialized states will not be those with the most solar, hydropower or wind potential—but those that can align energy, mining, industry, and trade policy; empower regulators with developmental mandates; and coordinate across borders.

Africa's green industrialization challenge isn't just skills [https://lnkd.in/ezHDdR-Y], demand [https://lnkd.in/esCpsRkC], capital structure [https://lnkd.in/eyZB2mZE] or politics [https://lnkd.in/eEtMdiWX]. It’s institutional: a deficit of governance muscle.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Hubert Nii-Aponsah, PhD Rex Asiama (PhD) Solomon Owusu Victor Osei Kwadwo, Ph.D. Rose Camille Vincent, Ph.D. Davina Osei Woubet Kassa, PhD Emmanuel Buadi Mensah
